# Data Analytics {#sec-analytics}

This section covers all analytical methods applied to the prepared data:
descriptive spatial analytics, predictive modelling of demand (SVM and
neural networks), and reinforcement learning for smart charging.

#### Shortfalls and Improvement Levers {#sec-svm-shortfalls}

<!-- DRAFT bullets for later revisiting -- expand into prose once the final
tables/figures (tbl-svr-level-comparison, fig-svr-feature-importance) are
embedded. Numbers below are from the completed 3.2a run
(models_predictions/SVR/standard/models/level_comparison.csv, permutation_importance_blocks.csv,
drop_column_ablation.csv). -->

- **The SVR barely beats, and at one of six granularities loses to, a
  historical-mean ("climatology") baseline.** Skill score
  (`1 - MAE_model / MAE_base_demand`) ranges from **+10.2%** (h3_7/daily, the
  best case) down to **-25.8%** (census/hourly, the worst); community/hourly is
  essentially a coin flip at +1.3%. Every level sits closer to break-even than
  to a clear win.
- **Daily aggregation beats hourly at every matching spatial resolution:**
  h3_7 (+10.2% daily vs. +5.8% hourly), census (+6.3% vs. **-25.8%**),
  community (+9.0% vs. +1.3%). The effect is largest at the coarsest spatial
  units, consistent with hourly bins being sparser and more sensitive to the
  balanced-sample/natural-prevalence mismatch noted below.
- **Permutation importance and drop-column ablation disagree — but only at the
  two coarsest, daily-aggregated levels, not everywhere.** At `census/daily` and
  `community/daily`, shuffling `base_demand` inflates MAE by **+53,170%** and
  **+4,989%** respectively (the fitted model leans on it almost entirely), yet
  retraining *without* it costs only **+1.1%** and **+4.6%** MAE — it is a
  pre-digested shortcut to `(cell, day_of_week)` information the model already
  has via `lat`/`lon`/`calendar` features, so dropping it is nearly free at
  these two levels.
  **At every other level this reliance is genuine, not redundant:** ablating
  `base_demand` costs +215.9% MAE at h3_7/hourly, +248.4% at census/hourly,
  +53.6% at community/hourly, and +169.9% at h3_7/daily — all clear,
  load-bearing drops. The "reliance without necessity" pattern is specific to
  few-large-area, coarse-temporal grids, not a general property of the model.
- **This ceiling is largely inherent to the assignment's own framing, not a
  fixable modeling error.** The brief explicitly rules out autoregressive
  prediction (hour x from hour x−1) in favor of scenario-conditioned prediction
  (cell + calendar + weather, e.g. "a rainy Sunday 10-11am on the outskirts").
  Under that constraint, cell + calendar features are close to the ceiling of
  what's predictable — a historical mean over those same keys is close to
  optimal, so there is limited room for a learned model to add value without
  reintroducing autoregressive signal, which is out of scope here.
- **Tested improvement lever — residual-on-baseline, tuned from scratch on the
  residual target — improves 5 of 6 levels, with one small regression traced to
  validation-selection variance, not the reframing itself.** Instead of fitting
  the SVR to predict `log1p(demand)` from scratch, we fit it to predict the
  log-space correction `log1p(demand) - log1p(base_demand)` and reconstruct
  `demand_hat = expm1(log1p(base_demand) + correction_hat)`, with the kernel and
  `C`/`gamma` search run directly on the residual target (not reused from the
  direct model) via a manual K-fold grid search (`GridSearchCV`'s scorer cannot
  reconstruct counts from a residual prediction without the row's
  `base_demand`, which it never sees). The gain is largest exactly where the
  direct model struggled most: `census/hourly` closes more than half its gap to
  zero (-25.8% → -13.3%, +12.6 points), and `community/hourly` flips from a
  coin-flip (+1.3%) to a clear win (+5.7%); `h3_7/hourly` and `h3_7/daily` each
  improve by ~3 points. One level gets slightly worse — `census/daily`
  (+6.3% → +6.1%) — where the from-scratch search picked a *different* feature
  set than the direct model, a sign of validation-selection variance at that
  noisier level rather than the residual target itself being worse: every level
  where the *same* feature set and kernel were re-evaluated with only the target
  changed showed a genuine improvement.
- **Other legitimate, non-autoregressive improvement levers for a follow-up:**
  - Weather × hour and weather × spatial interaction terms (currently weather
    is city-wide and hourly, i.e. no spatial variation across cells within the
    same hour).
  - Finer-grained or spatially-resolved weather data.
  - Richer POI features (e.g. distances to nearest POI of each category, not
    just aggregate counts per cell).
- **Negative skill is worst at the sparsest hourly level (census/hourly
  -25.8%), which may partly reflect a train/test distribution mismatch rather
  than pure model weakness:** training uses a class-balanced sample (roughly
  equal zero/non-zero rows) while test is evaluated at natural prevalence
  (~97%+ zeros at this level). Worth checking performance under
  natural-prevalence training before concluding the model is fundamentally
  unsuited to sparse grids.
- **Kernel choice is empirically justified, not just prescribed by the
  assignment:** every one of the 6 winning models selected an RBF kernel
  (C=10, gamma='scale') over linear or polynomial. A linear kernel's unbounded
  predictions in log-space explode through `expm1` back-transformation,
  producing catastrophic count-space errors — a concrete illustration of *why*
  a nonlinear kernel is needed for this target, not just a step to gradually add
  per the assignment recipe.

## Smart Charging (Reinforcement Learning) {#sec-rl}

An electric taxi driver charges at home. The vehicle arrives at 2 p.m. and leaves

<!-- STATUS: notebook 4.1 ReinforcementLearning.ipynb implements this task as a
tabular Q-learning MVP. It is WIP — several cells carry TODOs (describe the Env /
Agent / Training, vary alpha_t over time, add stronger baselines, multi-seed

We frame the taxi driver's home charging as a Markov Decision Process and solve it
with Q-learning. The agent sets the charging power in 15-minute steps between the
2 p.m. arrival and 4 p.m. departure, trading off recharging cost against the risk
of not meeting the (stochastic) energy demand for the working day.
